purpose: Rituximab-arrx is used to treat certain types of cancer, like non-Hodgkin lymphoma and chronic lymphocytic leukemia. It is also used for some autoimmune conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and microscopic polyangiitis. It helps control diseases where your immune system or abnormal blood cells are causing harm.
how_it_works: Your body has certain white blood cells called B cells, which carry a protein on their surface called CD20. This medication attaches to that CD20 protein and signals your immune system to destroy those B cells. By reducing the number of these B cells, it can slow down cancer growth or calm an overactive immune system that is attacking your own body.
common_side_effects: Infusion reactions during or shortly after the IV drip, such as fever, chills, nausea, headache, or rash. You may also experience fatigue, low blood counts (which can increase infection risk), and mild stomach upset. Some people notice body aches or swollen lymph nodes.
warnings: This medication carries serious warnings. It can cause severe, sometimes life-threatening infusion reactions, so you will be closely monitored during each treatment. It can reactivate hepatitis B virus in people who have had it before, which can be dangerous. There is also a rare but serious brain infection called PML. It can increase your risk of infections because it lowers your immune defenses. Tell your doctor about all vaccines, medications, and any signs of infection like fever or cough.
typical_dosing: This medication is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion in a clinic or hospital — you cannot take it at home as a pill. The dose and schedule depend on what condition is being treated. For many cancers, it may be given once a week for several weeks, or once every few weeks combined with chemotherapy. Your doctor will determine the exact dose and schedule that is right for you.
